ety.text: From Middle English eten, from Old English etan (“to eat”), from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną (“to eat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti, from *h₁ed- (“to eat”). Cognates Cognate with Scots ait (“to eat”), Yola ayth, eight (“to eat”), North Frisian iidj, iit, ää'e, ääre, ääse (“to eat”), Saterland Frisian iete, íete (“to eat”), West Frisian ite (“to eat”), Alemannic German asse, assu, essen, ässe, ässä (“to eat”), Bavarian eisn, essn, èssn (“to eat”), Cimbrian èssan, èzzan (“to eat”), Dutch and Low German eten (“to eat”), German essen (“to eat”), Luxembourgish iessen…

From Middle English ete, ate, æte, from Old English ǣt (“food, eating”), from Proto-West Germanic *āt, from Proto-Germanic *ētą (“food, thing to eat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”). Cognate with West Frisian iten (“food”), Saterland Frisian Íeten (“food”), German Aas (“carrion”), Vilamovian aosa (“food”), Icelandic át (“eating; solid food”).

senses.d: To consume (something solid or semi-solid, usually food) by putting it into the mouth and swallowing it.
ex: Don't disturb me now. Can't you see that I'm eating?
What time do we eat this evening?

senses.d: To have a particular quality of diet; to be well-fed or underfed.
ex: I try to eat healthy these days.
It's a soup that eats like a meal.

senses.d: To be savored or enjoyed; to taste in a specified way.
ex: It's an unattractive dish, but it eats pretty good.

senses.d: To destroy, consume, or use up.
ex: This project is eating up all the money.

senses.d: To consume (an exception, an event, etc.) so that other parts of the program do not receive it.
To damage, destroy, or fail to eject a removable part or an inserted object.
ex: The VHS recorder just ate the tape and won't spit it out.
John is late for the meeting because the photocopier ate his report.

senses.d: To consume money (or other instruments of value, such as a token) deposited or inserted by a user, while failing to either provide the intended product or service or return the payment.
ex: The video game in the corner just ate my quarter.
Hey! This stupid [soda vending] machine ate my quarter.

senses.d: Something to be eaten; a meal; a food item.

grp.label: to ingest — see also consume, ingest

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French manger, from Old French mengier, from Late Latin manducāre (“chew, devour”).
Borrowed from Old French mangier, from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of manducare, manicare, and manucare.
Inherited from Old Spanish comer, from Vulgar Latin *comēre, restructuring of Latin comedere.

es:morfar.gl: to gobble, to scoff, to scarf (to eat voraciously)

ety.text: Uncertain. Likely derived from Italian morfa. Possibly borrowed from French morfer (“to eat”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese comer, from Vulgar Latin *comēre, restructuring of Latin comedere. Cognate with Galician, Mirandese, Asturian, and Spanish comer and Mirandese quemer.
Literally, “to put under the teeth.” Compare French se mettre sous la dent.
Old French mangierbor. Italian mangiarebor. Spanish manyar Borrowed from Italian mangiare. Doublet of manducar.
Probably borrowed from Latin mandūcāre. Doublet of manjar.
From Old French rongier, from a crossing of rungier (from Latin rūmigāre (“chew”)) with influence from a Vulgar Latin *rodicāre, itself from Latin rōdō (“to gnaw”).
Inherited from Old French bouffer, originally "to puff up," from Medieval Latin buffa, itself echoic of puffing out cheeks.
From Middle English etynge, from Old English eting.

senses.d: Suitable to be eaten without being cooked.
ex: Wait! That's not an eating apple.
Arabs consider the eating of mushrooms as an aphrodisiac aid.
I remember when we visited Aunt Martha's house, we had some really good eating!

senses.d: The act of corroding or consuming some substance.

it:mangiare.gl: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: eating.

pt:comestível.gl: which can be eaten without harm; comestible, edible

ety.text: Borrowed from Medieval Latin comestibilis, from Latin comedō (“to eat”). Piecewise doublet of comível.
